newsitem.title: USA: Commonwealth backs off taking hard line on Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth backs off taking hard line on Nigeria.

text.p: Commonwealth ministers on Sunday backed away from antagonizing Nigeria, deciding instead to abandon talk of sanctions for the time being and send a fact-finding mission to the powerful oil-rich African state.

They also considerably softened their position on the fact-finding mission by scrapping an earlier insistence that Nigeria should guarantee Commonwealth officials access to opposition groups and human rights campaigners.
Given Nigeria's refusal to give the necessary assurances, the eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) decided some sort of dialogue was better than none at all.

"We weren't going to get guarantees. You can tell as much by who you don't see and who you're not allowed to see as by those you do see," said Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy, who had previously insisted on the guarantees.
Ministers, speaking after two days of talks on how to push Nigeria back into the democratic fold, said they hoped the visit would take place by the end of the year.
Axworthy eased his position to fit in with the rest of his colleagues, who have pursued a softer line on Nigeria.
CMAG agreed to a set of sanctions in April but suspended them until September to give Nigeria more chance for dialogue.
"Since we have decided to go to Nigeria the measures we approved will not be implemented," Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge told a news conference.
The Commonwealth, a grouping of Britain and its former colonies and protectorates, suspended Nigeria last November after it executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other human rights activists.

It made clear the suspension would stay in force until CMAG was fully able to investigate alleged human rights abuses in Nigeria. Last month CMAG scrapped a fact-finding mission when Nigeria denied access to opposition groups.
Mudenge said the ministers now trusted the military government of General Sani Abacha -- accused by critics of wide-scale human rights violations -- would let them speak to whomever they wanted.

"When we are in Nigeria we'll meet those people who have an opportunity to meet with us. We hope to have access to anyone who can be of help to us," he said, denying that the the Commonwealth was being soft on Nigeria.
"May I remind you that the Commonwealth suspended Nigeria. No other grouping has taken stronger measures than the Commonwealth," he said.
Nigeria insists on discussing its suspension from the Commonwealth before broaching other topics and has shown little desire to let Commonwealth ministers speak to opposition groups.
Axworthy's frustration with what he saw as foot-dragging by other members boiled over a few days ago when he denounced "appeasers" in the grouping, but on Sunday he sought to play down his remarks.

In June Canada unilaterally imposed the sanctions the action group had agreed on -- including a ban on sports links and arms sales -- but experts said the only measure to have any effect would be an worldwide embargo on oil sales.

Britain and New Zealand oppose the idea on the grounds that it would hurt ordinary Nigerians. And an embargo would only work with the support of the United States, which buys 40 percent of its oil from Nigeria.
The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group consists of Malaysia, Zimbabwe, Jamaica, Ghana, Britain, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada.
